Lissarca notorcadensis, a small bivalve mollusc endemic to Antarctic waters, exhibits a life history tightly constrained by the frigid conditions of its environment. Field surveys conducted at a stable water temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C] have provided key morphometric data for this species. The ultimate shell length, representing the maximum size attained by adults, approaches 0.8 centimetres [Li = 0.8 centimetres], a modest dimension that reflects the energetic limitations of polar existence. Newly metamorphosed juveniles settle at a shell length of just 0.0513 centimetres , indicating a remarkably small size at the completion of larval development. This tiny initial size, recorded in recently settled spat collected from bryozoan substrates, underscores the extreme compression of the early benthic phase in this species.

Reproductive investment in Lissarca notorcadensis is closely linked to body size. The threshold for reproductive activation, marking the onset of pubertal development, is achieved at a shell length of 0.38 centimetres [Lp = 0.38 centimetres], a size that individuals typically reach after several years of slow growth under near-freezing conditions. For an assumed adult shell length of 3 cm, the maximum reproductive rate has been estimated from fecundity data. Given the energetic constraints imposed by the ambient temperature of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], females produce approximately 57 eggs over the course of a year. When converted to a daily equivalent, this rate corresponds to roughly 0.156 eggs per day, though such a metric obscures the strongly seasonal spawning pattern observed in this polar species. The production of these eggs is likely tied to the short summer pulse of phytoplankton productivity.

Body mass parameters for Lissarca notorcadensis reveal a high degree of shell calcification relative to tissue content. The ultimate dry weight, representing the maximum somatic mass reached by fully mature adults, has been determined to be 0.0037 grams . This value was derived from direct measurements of desiccated tissue from large individuals collected near the Antarctic Peninsula. At the other extreme, the wet weight at birth, measured immediately following the hatching of the lecithotrophic veliger larva from its egg capsule, is exceptionally low at 0.00000572 grams [Wwb = 0.00000572 grams]. This minute initial mass, based on a recorded egg diameter of 254 micrometres, highlights the extremely limited yolk reserves available to the developing embryo.

Life span in Lissarca notorcadensis is remarkably extended given its diminutive size, a common feature of slow-growing polar invertebrates. The maximum documented longevity, recorded in individuals maintained under laboratory conditions that closely mimic the natural thermal regime of 2 °C [T = 2 °C], reaches 20 years [am = 20 years]. This considerable duration, equivalent to approximately 7300 days, allows the species to accumulate the energetic surplus necessary for repeated reproductive events. The long life span is thought to be an adaptation to the highly unpredictable and food-limited environment of the Southern Ocean, where successful recruitment may occur only infrequently. Such extreme longevity stands in contrast to the much shorter lives of temperate and tropical bivalves of similar ultimate shell length.

Comparisons with other Antarctic bivalves reveal that Lissarca notorcadensis occupies a distinctive ecological niche as an epibiotic brooder. Unlike many free-living infaunal species that release planktotrophic larvae, this species retains its developing offspring within the mantle cavity until the pediveliger stage is reached. The transition from brooded larva to an independent, crawling juvenile capable of byssal attachment occurs at a shell length of 0.0513 centimetres , a size that marks the end of the metamorphic process. Furthermore, the strong correlation between adult shell size and reproductive output is evident in the ultimate dry weight of 0.0037 grams , which presumably limits the number of eggs that can be simultaneously brooded within the restricted space of the mantle cavity. This brooding habit, coupled with the low thermal energy availability at 2 °C [T = 2 °C], reinforces the slow pace of life history events in this species.
